messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 60
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fisherman
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Thao

Thao was sixty-two when his youngest son, Minh, drowned during a fishing expedition off the coast of North Carolina. It was a summer morning in 2019, the kind of bright, ordinary day that Thao had known for forty years at sea. Minh, then twenty-eight, had wanted to learn the family trade—had insisted on it, in fact, over his mother's protests. They were checking nets three miles offshore when the current shifted. Minh, who had never been a strong swimmer despite growing up in a fishing family, lost his footing on the slick deck. Thao saw him go over the rail. He heard the splash. He dove, but the water was dark and cold, and by the time the Coast Guard arrived, Minh had been under for nearly ten minutes. They recovered his body two days later. At the funeral, Thao sat motionless in his dark suit, feeling nothing—or rather, feeling as though something essential had been hollowed out and replaced with a weight that would never lift.

In the months after Minh's death, Thao returned to fishing. His wife, Linh, had begged him not to. But the boat was how he had always made sense of the world, and the alternative—sitting at home with his grief—felt impossible. What he did not anticipate was that the water itself had become a landscape of danger. Within weeks of going back out, he began to experience sudden, overwhelming physical reactions. The smell of salt spray would trigger a racing heart and a sensation of drowning that lasted for hours. Once, when a younger crew member slipped on deck, Thao's hands began to shake so violently he had to sit down, gripping the rail until his knuckles whitened. He was certain something terrible was about to happen again—that the sea was waiting to take someone else, perhaps him, perhaps one of the men who depended on him. His sleep deteriorated. He would lie awake beside Linh, his body rigid with tension, replaying the moment of the splash over and over, wondering if there was something he should have seen, something he could have done differently. The anger came too, sudden and hot—at Minh for being careless, at himself for allowing his son on the boat, at God for the senselessness of it all.

What made everything worse was the certainty that had settled into Thao's mind: people could not be trusted to keep themselves safe, not even—or especially not—the ones you loved most. He had come to believe that vigilance was the only thing standing between his family and disaster. His wife had survived; his older son had survived. But they could be taken at any moment, and there was nothing he could do to prevent it. This belief hardened into something almost paranoid. When Linh mentioned going to the grocery store, Thao felt a spike of dread—what if something happened while she was driving? When his older son called late, Thao's first thought was that something had happened to him. These fears fed the physical reactivity that now governed his days. A car horn outside the house would send his heart into his throat. The sight of water—even the rain-filled gutter beside their driveway—could trigger that suffocating sensation of drowning, that certainty that death was close. And each time his body reacted this way, it confirmed what he now believed: the world was fundamentally unsafe, and the people around him were vulnerable in ways he could not control. He felt dead inside most of the time, as though the part of him that had died with Minh was the only part that had ever truly been alive. The guilt was relentless—he had survived, and Minh had not. Why? What had he done to deserve another day when his son would never have another?

Thao stopped going out on the boat regularly, though he could not admit this to his fishing crew. Instead, he found reasons to stay ashore—equipment repairs, administrative tasks, things that kept him from the water. His income dropped noticeably. Linh began working extra shifts at the hospital where she was a nurse, and the tension between them grew thick and silent. He withdrew from the Vietnamese community gatherings they had attended for decades, afraid of the questions, the sympathy, the inevitable conversations that would circle back to Minh. Now, at sixty-two, Thao sits in the waiting room of a therapist's office, referred by his primary care physician who had noted his blood pressure climbing steadily over the past three years. He is not sure why he agreed to come. Part of him believes that talking about what happened will only make it worse, that acknowledging the danger he feels will somehow invite it closer. But another part of him—the part that watches Linh's exhaustion, that hears the strain in his older son's voice when he calls—knows that something has to change. He is terrified that if he loosens his grip on the vigilance that has kept him alive, something catastrophic will happen. And he is equally terrified that he will feel this way forever, dead inside, unable to trust that anyone he loves will make it through another day.
